social.text: # music # musicproduction I have some old Now! CDs and a theory. So some songs, especially from the 2000s, sound muddy. For example: Daddy Yankee -- Gasolina Pussycat Dolls -- I Don't Need a Man Beyoncé -- Crazy In Love I looked at their spectrums in Audacity and compared them with We Are Never Getting Back Together, which sounds crystal-clear to me. The Taylor Swift song has much more energy in the higher frequencies. Also compared with Bastille's Pompeii to confirm my theory. Pompeii's thinner in the higher frequencies than We Are Never Getting Together, but there's a narrow band of high-intensity up top. Maybe that's why it sounds more balanced? Also, some songs don't sound like they give enough space between instruments. In Crazy in Love it sounds like everything's vying for centre stage. Do you think I'm right or is this something else? Something weird is that all these songs are from 2005-2007. Maybe there was some kind of compression SNAFU?

social.text: Eyeline 🎬 Eyeline is where a character looks, and it quietly steers how a scene reads. Cut from a character looking off-screen to what they’re looking at, and we see through their eyes. Matched eyelines also make actors filmed separately feel like they’re facing each other. On set: give actors a mark beside the lens and keep the eyeline clear. # Filmmaking # Cinematography # EyelineMatch # FilmTechnique # ContinuityEditing

social.text: Auteur theory 🎬 Auteur theory holds that a film’s director is its ‘author’: the creative force whose personal style and recurring themes run through their work. It began with critics at Cahiers du Cinéma in 1950s France (Truffaut, Godard) and was named by American critic Andrew Sarris in 1962. Critics push back that filmmaking is collaborative. Both views matter. # Filmmaking # AuteurTheory # FilmTheory # FrenchNewWave # FilmHistory

social.author: @macwinstudios@mastodon.social
social.text: Isolation shot vs two shot 🎬 Isolation shot (a clean single): one character alone in the frame. It focuses us on their emotion and can make them feel alone. Two shot: both characters in frame. It shows distance, closeness and power between them, and lets us watch one react while the other acts. Most dialogue scenes mix both. Go to singles too early, and it turns into ping-pong. # Filmmaking # Cinematography # TwoShot # FilmTechnique # Coverage

social.author: @macwinstudios@mastodon.social
social.text: Comedic framing 🎬 Comedy isn’t just in the script. It’s in where you put the camera. Go wide so physical gags play out in full. Use a two-shot to show contrast between characters. Cut to the reaction, because the reaction is often the punchline. Hold the reveal outside the frame, then show it. Timing in the frame matters as much as timing in the performance. # Filmmaking # Cinematography # VisualComedy # FilmTechnique # Comedy
